summary: This note is a Wikipedia-style article on the Sahara, the largest hot desert in the world and the third-largest desert overall, spanning North Africa. It covers the desert's geography and regions, its extreme hot and dry climate, temperature and rainfall extremes, and the prehistoric wet-dry cycles driven by orbital changes. It also describes ecoregions and flora and fauna, and the text ends mid-sentence in the fauna section.
one_line: Wikipedia-derived overview of the Sahara desert's geography, extreme climate, prehistoric wet-dry cycles, ecoregions, and wildlife across North Africa.
key_facts: The Sahara covers 9,200,000 square kilometres (3,600,000 sq mi) and is the largest hot desert in the world and the third-largest desert overall.
The name Sahara is derived from Arabic ṣaḥārā, a broken plural of ṣaḥrā', meaning desert.
The Sahara stretches from the Red Sea in the east and the Mediterranean in the north to the Atlantic Ocean in the west, and is bounded to the south by the Sahel.
For several hundred thousand years the Sahara has alternated between desert and savanna grassland in a 20,000-year cycle caused by the precession of Earth's axis.
Emi Koussi, a shield volcano in the Tibesti range of northern Chad, is the highest peak in the Sahara.
The eastern part of the Great Desert in the Libyan Desert is described as the sunniest, driest and most nearly rainless place on the planet, rivaling the Atacama Desert.

Bou Bernous, a remote desert town in the Algerian Desert at an elevation of 378 metres, recorded a world's highest officially recorded average daily high temperature of 47 °C (116.6 °F), and only Death Valley, California rivals it.
A sand temperature of 83.5 °C (182.3 °F) has been recorded in Port Sudan.
Most of the Sahara receives less than 20 millimetres (0.8 in) of rain annually, and the annual average rainfall can drop to less than 1 millimetre in the central hyper-arid core.
At least two instances of snowfall have been recorded in the Sahara, in February 1979 and December 2016, both in the town of Ain Sefra.
Lake Mega-Chad, which existed during the African humid period, is estimated to have covered 350,000 km2 at its largest extent, before 5000 BCE; Lake Chad is its remnant.
The Saharan flora comprises around 2800 species of vascular plants, approximately a quarter of which are endemic.
The Atlantic coastal desert covers 39,900 square kilometers in southern Morocco and Mauritania, where coastal fog from the Canary Current sustains lichens, succulents and shrubs.
The addax, a large white antelope, can go nearly a year in the desert without drinking.

entities.name: Sahara
entities.role: largest hot desert in the world, spanning North Africa, the subject of the note

entities.name: Sahel
entities.role: belt of semi-arid tropical savanna bounding the Sahara to the south

entities.name: Emi Koussi
entities.role: shield volcano in the Tibesti range of northern Chad and the highest peak in the Sahara

entities.name: Tibesti Mountains
entities.role: volcanic mountain range in northern Chad where Emi Koussi rises

entities.name: Bou Bernous
entities.role: remote desert town in the Algerian Desert with the world's highest officially recorded average daily high temperature, 47 °C

entities.name: Port Sudan
entities.role: location where a sand temperature of 83.5 °C was recorded

entities.name: Ain Sefra
entities.role: town where snowfall was recorded in February 1979 and December 2016

entities.name: Lake Mega-Chad
entities.role: paleolake that existed during the African humid period, of which Lake Chad is the remnant

entities.name: Atacama Desert
entities.role: desert in Chile and Peru that rivals the Libyan Desert in dryness

entities.name: Death Valley
entities.role: California location that alone rivals Bou Bernous in recorded heat

entities.name: Atlantic coastal desert
entities.role: narrow ecoregion along the Atlantic coast in southern Morocco and Mauritania

entities.name: Intertropical Convergence Zone
entities.role: continuous belt of low-pressure systems near the equator that is the primary source of rain in the Sahara and Sahel

entities.name: John Kutzbach
entities.role: meteorologist who formally proposed and tested the hypothesis that insolation drives long-term monsoon cycles in 1981

entities.name: Rudolf Spitaler
entities.role: late nineteenth-century thinker who first suggested insolation changes from Earth's orbit control monsoon strength

entities.name: Ruddiman
entities.role: author who named the Orbital Monsoon Hypothesis in 2001

entities.name: Robert Capot-Rey
entities.role: geographer whose climatic criteria are cited for the northern limit of the Sahara

entities.name: Great Green Wall
entities.role: African reforestation initiative, reported in August 2023 to have covered only 18% of its planned area

entities.name: Sahara pump theory
entities.role: theory describing how flora and fauna shift between the Sahara and surrounding regions during wet and dry cycles
